Oct 29 : Cash flow is king again. Wall Street rewarded Microsoft and Oracle on Wednesday for showing that they could fund their enormous AI ambitions without endlessly tapping investors. Alphabet, by contrast, was punished for burning through cash, while Google Search's slower growth fanned fears that competition was hurting the business that bankrolls its AI expansion. Microsoft shares jumped more than 3 per cent in after-hours trading, while Alphabet plunged nearly 10 per cent, as investors drew a sharper distinction between companies making money from AI and those struggling to contain its costs.

The divergence shows that after rewarding companies for spending aggressively to secure computing capacity — often through debt — investors are demanding more evidence that the resulting growth can finance the next round of outlays. Meta offered an early warning last week, when better-than-expected revenue growth and an upbeat outlook were eclipsed by its cash burn. Oracle, on the other hand, ended regular trading nearly 11 per cent higher on Wednesday after Larry Ellison's company said it was planning to put a ceiling on external financing and expected to turn its cash flow positive in the second half of fiscal 2028. "Alphabet and Microsoft were night and day," said Melissa Otto, head of research at S&P Global Visible Alpha. "Microsoft's quarter demonstrated very disciplined growth, whereas Google is burning cash and its core business came in below expectations," she said, adding that it may lead investors to question "is AI taking some share" from Google Search. Google's search revenue grew 12 per cent in the September quarter but fell short of expectations for a 14.7 per cent increase, even as CEO Sundar Pichai said queries were growing at their fastest pace in five years. The long-lucrative business is under threat from AI chatbots and agents that are changing how people search for information, just as the company pours more money into the technology. Capital expenditure will increase significantly in 2027, CFO Anat Ashkenazi told analysts. CLOUD BOOM, CASH SQUEEZE Alphabet's eyebrow-raising capital outlay — with as much as $205 billion expected this year — is, however, driving gains at Google's other major AI business. Google Cloud revenue more than doubled to $30.71 billion, but Alphabet's spending overwhelmed that growth. Cash burn hit $9.07 billion after the company posted its first quarter of negative cash flow in the June period. "This is definitely a different business, Google. It's a different business today than it was three, five, 10 years ago," said Jeremy Saltzberg, vice president and senior investment officer at Check Capital, which owns Alphabet shares. Saltzberg pushed back on the concerns about spending, saying Alphabet needed to have big outlays to stay competitive at a time when OpenAI and Anthropic appear to be pulling ahead in Silicon Valley's AI model race. "We think this is a sport of kings, which is that if you don't have $150 billion to spend next year on capital expenditure, don't even bother showing up," Saltzberg said. MICROSOFT'S CASH FLOW ADVANTAGE Microsoft offered a stark contrast. The company generated $18.6 billion in free cash flow in its fiscal first quarter, nearly $10 billion more than Wall Street expected, even as it poured $45.2 billion into expanding its computing infrastructure. Revenue at its Azure cloud business surged a better-than-expected 48 per cent and the company forecast faster-than-expected cloud growth for the current quarter, suggesting corporate demand for AI computing remains strong. The results also suggested Microsoft was finding a broader market for AI beyond a handful of deep-pocketed customers, including OpenAI, whose heavy computing requirements have fueled the industry's expansion. "The shiny object stuff is waning" as more businesses move beyond experimenting with the newest or most powerful AI models and commit to long-term contracts, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said in a conference call with analysts. "I want the breadth," he said. "We have large customers who want to buy from us ... As long as the pricing is right, we may sell them some. If not, we will be patient about building the breadth business."

Source: Reuters

SEOUL, Oct 29 : A South Korean court on Thursday rejected a lawsuit by dozens of Tesla owners seeking full refunds for money paid for "Full Self-Driving" driver-assistance software, ruling that the automaker had not breached its contractual obligations. The Seoul Central District Court ruled against the 88 plaintiffs, finding that the FSD option did not promise fully autonomous driving without human intervention and that Tesla had already provided some of the functions included in the package. The court said Tesla's obligation to deliver additional features depended on technological advances and regulatory approvals, adding that buyers had been aware that some functions could take considerable time to become available. It also found that Tesla had provided basic Autopilot and Enhanced Autopilot functions, while a recent software update had added traffic light and sign recognition, as well as city-driving capabilities, to older vehicles equipped with Hardware 3 (HW3) computers.

SYDNEY, Oct 29 : Australia's corporate regulator said on Thursday it was probing the failed $5 billion initial public offering of AI data centre operator Firmus. Australian Securities and Investments Commission Chair Sarah Court said the regulator was yet to launch an official investigation, but said it had engaged with the banks leading the share sale. Firmus' planned IPO, due to be the second largest ever in Australia, collapsed on October 9 after failing to gain enough investors backing. The Nvidia-backed AI data center operator had planned to raise $5 billion in the IPO to value the company at $30.6 billion, triple the value achieved during a private fund raising round in August.

WASHINGTON, Oct 28 : The leak website Distributed Denial of Secrets said on Wednesday it has released data on more than 40,000 Department of Homeland Security employees, including details about officials working in sensitive fields such as surveillance and human intelligence. DHS said in a statement it was "aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively." The agency said it was working to ensure its employees were properly protected and would update the public "when more information is available.” The disclosure — which the nonprofit data transparency group says draws on information obtained by an entity calling itself "Department of Peace" — is the third major government data leak to have made headlines in the past month. In September, the hacking group ShinyHunters claimed the theft of a massive trove of data from the Federal Bureau of Investigation, including sensitive job details and medical information from thousands of bureau employees. Last week, the Defense Department was hit with a class action lawsuit following a breach that exposed data on millions of current and former military personnel.

The DHS data includes names, phone numbers and email addresses of employees from Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Customs and Border Protection, Homeland Security Investigations, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, and other DHS component agencies. Also included in the data were job titles and email groups, which, among other details, showed which agents were assigned to special operations, surveillance jobs, computer forensics and undercover work. In a statement, Distributed Denial of Secrets co-founder Emma Best said the hacktivist and journalist known as "maia arson crimew" developed a search tool for the data that would allow the public to browse it. Best said the tool would "replace anonymity with accountability" and empower journalists, guide public records requests and boost congressional oversight. Crimew said her tool would provide "FOIA material for years to come!" The Department of Peace did not immediately respond to a request for comment, but in a statement included with the data it said that DHS employees "have our information, so it's only fair that we have theirs" and that it hoped the data "can be used to limit further harm by the DHS and supports all efforts in that direction." The Department of Peace in March claimed responsibility for hacking DHS and posting documents related to contracts with outside vendors. Best's statement said the Department of Peace harvested the data from the Okta sign-on service used by DHS. Reuters could not immediately corroborate the claim. Okta said in response to a Reuters query: "Okta is secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised." Reuters could not immediately verify the authenticity of the entire data trove but it was able to match personal information about six DHS employees named in the leak to credit bureau records and breach data carried by the dark web intelligence platform District 4 Labs. Reuters called three DHS employees directly and was able to confirm their phone numbers and other details. One said it was the first they had heard of a breach. In several cases, the data tracked information available on DHS employees' LinkedIn profiles. But in others, the data revealed nonpublic data about internal DHS organization charts or previously undisclosed programs or operations.

NEW YORK, Oct 28 : Truth Social, the social media platform founded by President Donald Trump, has signed up news and data provider Bloomberg and two Wall Street firms for faster access to the president’s posts, which it sells for up to $100,000 a month, according to people with direct knowledge of the matter. The firms are Susquehanna International Group and Jump Trading, both high-frequency trading firms focused on algorithmic and automated strategies. The service gives subscribers a timing advantage to Trump's posts on Truth Social, which has the potential to create swings in financial markets and to give Wall Street traders an edge not available to everyday investors. The companies’ purchase of the Truth API service hasn’t been previously reported. An API is a programming interface that is used as a digital bridge that allows one system to connect to another. Trump Media and Technology Group announced its fastest-access product in July, and pitched it to trading firms and other financial institutions. The deals likely mark the first time a business tied to a sitting president has sold access to their statements, which some critics have called unethical.

While Truth Social’s pay-for-access plan ventures into untested legal territory, Intercept Media and the Freedom of the Press Foundation sued Trump in August, seeking to block the White House from posting official government announcements exclusively on Truth Social while the paid feed exists. The suit, which is ongoing, alleges that erecting a financial barrier to government information is potentially unconstitutional and favors wealthy Wall Street firms. Bloomberg, Jump Trading and Susquehanna declined to comment.  In a statement, Trump Media said: “Truth Social offers an industry-standard API product for which there is significant demand across industries. We take customer confidentiality seriously. This reporting is based on misleading information being peddled by anonymous sources aimed at harming our company, customers and shareholders.” The president’s family trust owns 41 per cent of Trump Media, and Trump is the trust’s sole beneficiary. Shares of the company have fallen more than 50 per cent so far this year. The market value of Trump Media has been volatile since it went public; it closed at about $8 billion in its March 2024 debut, but is now worth about $1.8 billion. The company has lost about $1.76 billion since 2024, including non-cash charges. Trump Media’s Securities and Exchange Commission filings listTrump, Jr., as the trustee of the family trust, with sole voting and investment power.  White House spokesman Davis Ingle said neither Trump nor his family is directly involved in any portfolio investment decisions but did not address the allegations that the president was improperly using his office. Trump Jr. did not respond to a comment request. Questions about his role in the business were referred to the Trump Organization, which did not respond to requests for comment.  MARKET-MOVING POSTS  The service is designed to allow customers to read Trump's posts more quickly than a human would by constantly checking the app. The timing advantage, described as 50 milliseconds by Trump Media officials, can matter to trading firms or financial news and data organizations because a US president’s posts can create swings in the value of assets. High-frequency Wall Street traders employ software that ingests news headlines, company announcements and government statements to search for market-moving information. The software can read, analyze and execute a trade in thousandths of a second. In one example of how Trump's posts can move markets, oil futures sank after he announced on Truth Social a ceasefire in the Iran war in April. In August, Trump Media told investors it had "signed more than 10 customer agreements” which Reuters was unable to confirm. The company didn’t name the clients, but said they were primarily Wall Street trading firms that are paying between $60,000 and $100,000 a month. Reuters, a financial-news competitor to Bloomberg, said in a statement: "We will assess the service, but have no current plans to subscribe." Selling faster access to Trump's posts has drawn criticism from Democrats and media entities. Democratic Senators Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts and California's Adam Schiff said in July that they had asked the US Securities and Exchange Commission to investigate whether the service violated securities laws. They described it as a “shocking abuse” of office by a president seeking personal gain, without providing further explanation. The SEC declined to comment. A TMTG spokesperson said, “Congressional Democrats continue to mischaracterize Truth API either out of ideological opposition to free markets or a failure to grasp the distinction between public and nonpublic information.”  In the lawsuit against Trump by Intercept Media and non-profit Freedom of the Press Foundation, the plaintiffs described the paid data service as "profoundly corrupt." The suit also alleges the service would violate the First Amendment rights of the public who don’t have equal access to the information and it would violate the Fifth Amendment by charging “unreasonable sums”  for equal access to information guaranteed by law.   The White House’s Ingle did not directly address the lawsuit or its allegations, saying,  “President Trump only acts in the best interests of the American public – which is why they overwhelmingly re-elected him to this office.”

NEW YORK, Oct 28 : The Federal Election Commission restored its electronic filing system Wednesday night after taking it offline for nearly 41 hours to contain a cyberattack, which temporarily concealed spending from big donors as political donations ramp up in the final days of the midterms.  Campaign watchdogs sounded alarms as the outage dragged into its third evening. Super PACs and other groups could not file mandatory 24- and 48-hour reports that show how much money they are spending to help or hurt candidates at the polls, shrouding the most recent political spending from public view. "We didn't have access to the last-minute spending, which is really ramped up as the election draws nearer," said campaign finance watchdog Molly White, who tracks crypto and Big Tech political spending. "We have no visibility into that when the filing systems are down." "It's pretty devastating this close to the election," she added.

The outage came at a critical time as daily spending accelerates to its fastest pace in the two-year election cycle, campaign finance experts said. Super PACs, which can accept and give unlimited amounts of money, and dark money groups spent an average of over $50 million per day the week before the outage, OpenSecrets research director Brendan Glavin said. More than $250 million in spending was reported on October 20 alone, he added. The FEC told users that most of the services affected by the outage have been restored. It posted a notice just after 10 p.m. ET on Monday saying it was investigating a problem that caused "major" outages across its systems that process electronic campaign filings.  Reuters could not establish the motive for the hacking effort. Hackers of all stripes regularly target government networks for espionage, financial gain or political motives. The FEC does not play a role in administering US elections and the outage should have no effect on voters' ability to cast ballots. “Disclosure delayed is disclosure denied,” Hilary Braseth, executive director of nonpartisan campaign finance watchdog OpenSecrets, said in a statement released before the system was restored. “When hundreds of millions of dollars in outside money flood political airwaves in the final days before an election, transparency is not an optional luxury, it is a fundamental public safeguard.” The FEC did not return requests for comment Wednesday and did not announce any details on the cause of the outage. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency and the FBI both referred questions to the FEC.  An FEC officer told campaign compliance firms late Monday that it took those services offline after a "bad actor" tried to breach the agency's systems, according to an email reviewed by Reuters. Campaign finance managers had to reset their passwords before logging in to the system, according to an email reviewed by Reuters.  The timing of the hacking attempt this close to the November 3 elections, and lack of information from the FEC, stirred up conspiracy theories throughout the industry, several people said. White noted that it would be a good way for unscrupulous actors to hide unpopular last-minute spending.  "It's hard to say with any real information that that's what happened, but it's certainly I think where people's minds go very quickly," she said. Kyle Sandy, the cybersecurity director at IT security firm Logically, said taking the system offline is the right call when dealing with an attack. "It tells me the FEC detected something they couldn't immediately scope and chose a known outage over an unknown risk," Sandy said, giving the agency time to ensure none of its data was altered by the hackers before bringing it back online.

Oct 28 : Microsoft on Wednesday forecast fiscal second-quarter cloud growth and overall sales that beat Wall Street estimates, sending shares up more than 5 per cent in after-hours trading. The forecast came after Microsoft had earlier beaten expectations for first-quarter cloud revenue, offering fresh evidence that its hefty AI investments were paying off as Wall Street grows increasingly wary of Big Tech's debt-fueled spending. The software and cloud company also generated $18.6 billion in free cash flow in its fiscal first quarter ended September — some $10 billion more than analysts expected — as capital spending came in below the company's own forecast and Microsoft's Azure cloud computing business surged 48 per cent. Microsoft said it expects second-quarter Azure growth of 49 per cent to 50 per cent, above analyst estimates of 47.6 per cent, according to Visible Alpha data. The company forecast overall sales of $96 billion to $97.1 billion, above estimates of $95.6 billion, according to LSEG data.

That financial firepower set Microsoft apart from rivals such as Alphabet and Meta, whose heavy AI investments have squeezed free cash flow and increased their reliance on borrowing. Alphabet reported negative free cash flow of $9.07 billion in the third quarter as capital spending jumped, overshadowing a doubling of its cloud sales and sending its shares down 8 per cent in extended trading. Microsoft shares have risen about 9 per cent so far this year, through Wednesday's close. Its five-year credit default swaps — a measure of perceived default risk — remain the tightest among the largest tech companies, according to Truist, even as spreads have widened across much of the AI trade. The results also show Microsoft capitalizing on corporate demand for AI, easing fears that the technology threatens its software empire and that its AI fortunes are too closely tied to unprofitable OpenAI. On a conference call with analysts, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said that "the shiny-object stuff is waning" in the AI market, with a broad set of Microsoft customers now making plans for spending over a decade or more, rather than a handful of large customers making quarter-by-quarter purchases. "That's what I've been waiting for, as opposed to four customers who buy a lot of capacity from you, and you can show a few quarters of growth," Nadella said. "That's not a business, as far as I'm concerned. I want the breadth." Nadella also said the company is seeking to give customers a range of AI options, some of them at lower cost than cutting-edge AI models. The company is trying to make its Copilot products more useful with each model release by "consolidating the frontier gains for broad deployment," he added. STRONG AZURE GROWTH "Microsoft's first-quarter report was about as clean as it gets for a company this size," said Jesse Cohen, senior analyst at Investing.com. "After Meta's and Alphabet's numbers revived AI-spending anxiety, this is the counterweight. Demand still exceeds supply, the commercial backlog is enormous, and returns are finally showing up in earnings and overall revenue." Last month, Microsoft said it would disclose Azure revenue in dollars, instead of just growth rates, offering a clearer picture of how its cloud business stacks up against rivals Amazon Web Services and Google Cloud. Revenue at Microsoft's Azure cloud computing business grew to $33.17 billion in the quarter, topping Visible Alpha's estimate of $32.84 billion. Overall revenue rose by a fifth to $92.28 billion, and an adjusted profit of $4.89 per share beat an average estimate of $4.73 a share. LOWER SPENDING THAN FORECAST Capital expenditure for the quarter rose to $45.2 billion from $34.9 billion in the year-ago period, but came in below the company's own projection of $50 billion. So far in calendar 2026, Microsoft's capital expenditure has been $118.1 billion, which means it would have to spend $56.9 billion in the final three months of the year to hit its own forecast of $175 billion given in July. Jonathan Neilson, Microsoft's vice president of investor relations, attributed the lower-than-expected capital expenditure to delays rather than any changes to the company's underlying spending plans. "We did see some third-party capacity deliveries that we expected in first quarter were actually delayed," Neilson said. Earlier on Wednesday, hyperscaler Oracle said it expects capital spending to peak this fiscal year and next, but pledged to raise no more than $20 billion in additional financing for AI through fiscal 2030. Overall, Big Tech is expected to pump more than $700 billion this year into building data centers and securing the hardware and energy needed to develop and run AI technologies. While faster revenue growth at these companies indicates their bets could be paying off, concerns over the cost of financing the outlay have heightened over the past few weeks. Shrinking cash flows and rising debt loads at US tech companies, including recent stress at neocloud company CoreWeave as well as record-high costs to insure Meta's debt against default, have added to market turmoil.

Oct 28 : Google parent Alphabet reported disappointing results in the core business of search advertising and a massive acceleration in cash burn as it poured resources into building out AI. In a sign of corporate customers embracing the technology, Google Cloud revenues more than doubled, but investors unnerved by the huge price tag and a growth slowdown in the market-dominating search engine sent shares down 10 per cent after hours. "In a market worried about AI cannibalizing the franchise, investors need to see search accelerating, not decelerating," said Dave Wagner, portfolio manager at Aptus Capital Advisors. "Cloud is carrying the story, but until search shows AI is additive, the stock's probably going to trade lower."

The Mountain View, California company reported negative free cash flow of $9.1 billion, versus analyst expectations that it would come close to breaking even, LSEG data showed. Aggressive efforts to boost cloud capacity and fund AI development led Alphabet to burn $5.9 billion last quarter, the first time it went into the negative in 22 years as a public company. Total revenue missed Wall Street targets: revenue growth for Google Cloud outpaced expectations but was not enough to offset a $1.4-billion miss in advertising. Alphabet's second straight quarter of negative cash flow was a sharp turn for a company that was long one of the tech sector's most prolific cash generators. Moreover, Alphabet still plans to significantly increase its 2027 capital expenditures from this year's spending forecasts of $195 billion to $205 billion, Chief Financial Officer Anat Ashkenazi told analysts on a conference call. While executives did not put a number on 2027 outlays, investors were nervous about a big jump. "A $300-billion (capex) number could potentially scare the market because free cash flow now is finally negative," said Jeremy Saltsburg, senior investment officer at Check Capital. In contrast, rival Microsoft, which also reported results on Wednesday, saw shares rise more than 5 per cent, fueled by positive free cash flow that outstripped analyst estimates. Ashkenazi added that she expected near-term margin pressure from the use of third-party cloud capacity. Net income available to common Alphabet shareholders fell 25 per cent to $26.17 billion, and adjusted earnings per share of $2.67 missed Wall Street targets of $3.02. The results reflect the huge costs of the AI buildout, with investors concerned both by potential overspending and the risk of falling behind rivals by not spending enough. Total third-quarter revenue of $127.6 billion fell short of analysts' estimate of $128.2 billion, LSEG data showed. Revenue from ads came in at $82 billion, missing expectations of $83.4 billion. Chief business officer Philipp Schindler attributed a larger-than-expected deceleration in search advertising growth to greater use of AI Mode, a chatbot interface for the search engine with which the company is still experimenting on ads. Google would begin rolling out advertisements in AI Mode to international markets, Schindler told a conference call. CLOUD INFLUENCE GROWS Alphabet attempted to offset the disappointing advertising performance by playing up its cloud computing unit, most notably by debuting Thomas Kurian, CEO of Google Cloud, as a speaker on the earnings call. Revenue at Google Cloud exceeded estimates and more than doubled to $30.71 billion in the third quarter ended September 30. Kurian said sales of Google's tensor processing units (TPUs), which compete with Nvidia's GPU chips, had become a meaningful contributor to his business unit. Alphabet started recognizing revenue from direct sales of what it called its "TPU Systems", spanning not only the chips but also associated hardware and software, last quarter. But Ashkenazi cautioned that the buildout of TPU inventory would further place pressure on free cash flow. Google Cloud's backlog had grown to $561 billion and Alphabet expected to recognize more than 55 per cent of it as revenue in the next 24 months, she added. The third-largest cloud services provider globally after Amazon Web Services and Microsoft's Azure, Google Cloud has expanded enterprise commitments, supported by multi-year cloud and AI infrastructure deals across cybersecurity, retail and financial services. Alphabet, Microsoft, Amazon, and Meta are projected to collectively spend well over $700 billion in 2026 to expand AI data center footprint, chips and high-performance networking capacity. In the face of supply bottlenecks for advanced silicon and data center power, Alphabet's investments in custom tensor processing units alongside third-party GPUs have helped expand its service delivery capabilities. Earlier on Wednesday, Google sought to preempt the results and counter a perception of losing out in the AI race by unveiling the new Gemini 4 Carbon model. This meant the company was again "leading at the frontier," CEO Sundar Pichai said on the call. Afterwards, analysts at Bernstein asked in a note, "Did Google rush the deployment of Gemini 4 models as an offset to softer financial metrics? And are the models ready for commercial deployment?"

WASHINGTON, Oct 28 : Scientists using a Chile-based telescope have identified an icy object orbiting beyond Pluto that may join our solar system's small roster of dwarf planets. Researchers said the candidate, named 2026 ED138, has a diameter estimated at between roughly 370 and 930 miles (600 and 1,500 km) and is orbiting about 46 times farther from the sun than Earth. By way of comparison, Pluto orbits at an average of about 40 times farther from the sun than Earth. The object was spotted using the new Vera C. Rubin Observatory, on the summit of the Cerro Pachón mountain in central Chile. The telescope is a joint initiative of the US National Science Foundation and US Department of Energy. Further observations are needed to confirm that the object is a dwarf planet.

If confirmed, 2026 ED138 would join five other dwarf planets recognized by the International Astronomical Union, the global authority on classifying celestial bodies. Those are Pluto, Eris, Haumea and Makemake, all of which orbit beyond the outermost planet Neptune, and Ceres, located in the main asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter. Based on the current data, 2026 ED138 would be among the largest of the dwarf planets. "For me, what this demonstrates is that many exciting discoveries remain to be made with the Rubin Observatory and other telescopes," said astrophysicist Matt Holman of the Center for Astrophysics, Harvard & Smithsonian, who first spotted 2026 ED138. Pluto long was considered the solar system's ninth and outermost planet, but was reclassified by the International Astronomical Union as a dwarf planet in 2006 because it did not meet the organization's formal definition of a planet. Pluto and the new dwarf planet candidate reside in a frigid region of the solar system populated by various icy bodies. There are still questions about the size and composition of 2026 ED138. To be considered a dwarf planet, an object must possess sufficient mass for its own gravity to pull it into a round shape. 2026 ED138 appears to have sufficient mass for that, but more observations are needed. "The main thing we need to do is to establish the physical size of 2026 ED138," Holman said. "When we observe with Rubin, we are seeing the sun's light reflected from the object," Holman said. "A smaller, more reflective object would show the same amount of light as a larger, less reflective object. Fortunately, by looking at longer wavelengths, with an observatory like ALMA, we can detect the light emitted by the object itself," which is helpful in measuring an object's size. ALMA, or the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array, is a powerful telescope also based in Chile. The discovery was announced at a scientific meeting in Spokane, Washington.

The binary "yes" or "no" bets in prediction markets are influencing the way retail investors speculate on high-profile IPOs, allowing traders to wager on aspects such as the closing prices and its listing venue without the need to buy shares. "Prediction market interest in Anthropic's IPO is the financial equivalent of people lining up outside the Apple Store before a new iPhone release," said Michael Ashley Schulman, a partner at wealth management and financial advisory firm Cerity Partners. Earlier this week, Anthropic took a major step toward going public by unveiling its IPO filing. The listing could value the AI lab behind the Claude models at between $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion, Reuters has reported.

Combined, the markets have attracted tens of millions of dollars in volume. "It is a healthy sign of robust interest and the wagers placed may help the market zero in on its eventual public market opening price," said Schulman. Prediction markets allow users to buy and sell contracts tied to the outcome of real-life events, with prices fluctuating as traders weigh the odds of the different outcomes. Once largely tied to politics and economic data, the platforms are increasingly moving into traditional Wall Street turf, offering tens of thousands of markets on stock moves, company data and other corporate events that often drive shares, Reuters reported last month.
